title: Carol Countdown 2026: The Festive Four need your votes
summary: It’s March Madness in a Christmas sweater. “Joy to the World,” “Carol of the Bells,” “Silent Night” and “O Holy Night” are still standing. Your vote decides who makes the championship.
content: Alyssa Gonzalez/CPR Roll the tape, Shipmates! It’s March Madness in a Christmas sweater, and this is CPR Classical’s 2026 Carol Countdown: The Festive Four. [Cue SportsCenter-style music — da-da-dun, da-da-dun.] Every bracket needs a Cinderella, and ours came with wings: “Angels We Have Heard on High” pulled off an upset over “White Christmas” in Round 2. The crowd went wild. Bing Crosby demanded a replay. Then the Angels ran into “Carol of the Bells.” The Bells knocked them out 59.2% to 40.8% in the closest contest of the quarterfinals. Tough day for a team that showed up with its own wings. Cinderella’s going home, my friend. Elsewhere in the bracket, “Joy to the World” got past “The First Noel,” 62.8% to 37.2%, and “O Holy Night” topped “Coventry Carol,” 62.1% to 37.9%. And the loudest score in the building? That came from “Silent Night.” It sent “Winter Wonderland” a-packin’ 64.1% to 35.9% — the widest margin of the round. So much for home-ice advantage. Four heavyweights. Two tickets to the championship. You get to decide who wins. Get off the bench, Shipmate, and vote for your favorites today! I’m Kabin Thomas, and this is CPR Classical’s Carol Countdown: The Festive Four. [Cue music — da-da-dun, da-da-dun.] Vote in our interactive bracket for Round 4 to help decide which carols advance and get entered to win a family four-pack of tickets to the Colorado Symphony’s “A Classical Christmas” on Dec. 5, at 7:30 p.m. See sweepstakes rules here . Fourth-round voting starts on Nov. 26 and is open until midnight Nov. 30. We’ll announce the carols that move on and open voting for Round 5 on Dec. 3. Voting will continue until we declare a champion on Tuesday, Dec. 8. Listen to CPR Classical’s Carol Countdown on Tuesday, Dec. 8, starting at 10 a.m., with the winner announced at 1 p.m. Listen for the Sound of the Season right after Thanksgiving on CPR Classical — your home for the holidays. Hear us in Denver at 88.1FM, listen online at CPRClassical.org , or tell your smart speaker to “Play CPR Classical.” “Carol Countdown” is a registered trademark of Colorado Public Radio.

title: Dress for Success offers women rentering the workforce free business attire
summary: The non-profit provides donated clothes to women who've been away from the workforce, whether that be from incarceration or homelessness, and those facing financial barriers.
content: Belinda had been out of the workforce for about seven years because she was fighting an addiction, but she recently found a job. Earlier this month, she went to a 5,000-square-foot clothing warehouse in University Hills Plaza and came out with fresh gear to wear for her new position. And she didn’t spend a dime. Dress for Success , an international non-profit with a center in South Denver, provides free clothing that will help women slip seamlessly back into the workforce. Kevin J. Beaty/Denverite Dress for Success Denver’s showroom of lightly used women’s clothing in University Hills. Aug. 27, 2026. Ad: “She actually was in a drug and alcohol treatment facility,” said the Colorado chapter CEO, Amara Martin. “She was just released after completing the program, and she is in transitional housing. Her case manager brought her down because she [was] starting a job on [a] Monday, and she’s very nervous because she hasn’t needed clothes. She felt like she didn’t look the part. She felt like she looked like what she had been through,” she said. Courtesy: Amara Martin Amara Martin, CEO of Dress For Success Denver, which has been open for about 20 years. That changed within a few hours. “Our personal stylist volunteers put her in some beautiful items: a gorgeous black pencil skirt, a black kitten heel, a little red jacket and she got a lovely scarf to go with it as well as a piece of jewelry,” Martin said. Belinda is one of about 250 women served by Dress for Success every month by Martin and about 60 volunteers. The organization is celebrating its 20th year in Colorado. The clothes come from the community. On the second Saturday of each month, people with women’s business clothes in good condition who want to donate them pack their vehicles with the garments, drive up to the building, and within 10 minutes, volunteers come to the car and unload the clothes. About 150 cars show up each month, Martin said. Elaine Tassy/CPR News Volunteers unload donations at Dress For Success Denver’s headquarters in the city’s University Hills neighborhood. Nov. 14, 2026. Dress for Success serves women who are returning to the workforce after a time away. That could be because of incarceration, homelessness, drug dependency or recently graduating from college or an educational program, Martin said. During the week, people like Belinda can come in and, depending on what they have lined up work-wise, can pick up different amounts of clothing. “If you are coming for an interview, you receive six pieces of clothing, one pair of shoes, one handbag, one wallet, five accessories, and three toiletry items,” Martin said. Kevin J. Beaty/Denverite Shoes fill racks inside Dress for Success Denver’s showroom of lightly used women’s clothing in University Hills. Aug. 27, 2026. Those who are a little farther along in the job-reentry process can get even more: “You have an internship or a temporary position; that is nine pieces of clothing, one pair of shoes, one wallet, one handbag, five accessories, and three toiletry items. And then if you’re here [because you’ve gained] employment … you get 12 pieces of clothing, two pairs of shoes, wallets, handbags, five accessories, and five toiletry items at absolutely no cost,” Martin said. Most people find out about the program through other community-based organizations. “Workforce centers, shelters, community corrections [and] schools have us listed as one of their partners. We have about 180 organizations that we are working with in the Denver Metro area,” she said. The next donation date is Saturday, Dec. 12 from 10 a.m. until 2 p.m., and Martin said they’re especially in need of clothes sizes 16 and larger. Kevin J. Beaty/Denverite Dress for Success Denver’s headquarters in University Hills. Aug. 27, 2026.

title: Why higher oil prices haven’t lifted Colorado production
summary: While the war with Iran has driven global oil prices higher, that has not yet translated into more oil production in Colorado.
content: While the war with Iran has driven global oil prices higher, that has not yet translated into more oil production in Colorado. The global supply decrease that began earlier this year has pushed oil above $100 a barrel at times. From March to August, U.S. crude oil production rose 1.7%, while Colorado’s fell 1.7%, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The reason: the amount of time and money required to expand production makes short-term disruptions an unprofitable basis for ramping up drilling or pumping. “Our investment decisions are based on long-term competitiveness rather than short-term commodity price movements,” Kim McHugh, a vice president of Chevron, said in a statement. Occidental Petroleum told investors in August that it was shifting some drilling from Colorado’s Denver-Julesburg Basin to Wyoming’s Powder River Basin, where its wells were outperforming the basin average. The Colorado Oil and Gas Association said state permitting timelines help explain why drillers haven’t responded more quickly to higher prices. “It is very, very difficult for Colorado to respond in real time to current market conditions because of our permitting timelines,” said Lynn Granger, the president of COGA. The Colorado Energy and Carbon Management Commission said the median time from submission of an oil and gas development plan to a commission decision was 236 days. The agency said that as of Nov. 19, operators had state approval to drill 655 oil and gas wells across Colorado. It attributed recent shifts in rig counts and well starts to more efficient drilling and the maturity of the Denver-Julesburg Basin. What companies are doing Trisha Curtis, CEO of the energy analysis firm PetroNerds, said large publicly traded companies like Chevron and Occidental Petroleum now dominate drilling in Colorado because they have the resources to navigate onerous state regulations. “Smaller operators absolutely would’ve, day one, they would’ve said, ‘Let’s increase output,’” said Curtis. Large operators, however, tend to be more cautious, even if they have permits approved to drill more. “They’re not going to drill through those permits just because they have a few months of high oil prices,” said Curtis. “They’re going to have a very steady as you go plan.” Ian Lange, an economics professor at the Colorado School of Mines, said that Colorado’s regulations may favor large operators, but that doesn’t necessarily explain lower production. He said North Dakota provides a useful comparison to Colorado in terms of production. From March to August, North Dakota’s oil production rose 3.4%. In August, North Dakota’s oil production was still 23% below its 2019 monthly peak, and Colorado’s was 21% below its own, according to EIA data. “Whatever you want to say about North Dakota, I’m guessing you’re not going to claim they have the same environmental regulations as Colorado,” said Lange. In Colorado, “if they want to drill some more, they can drill some more,” said Lange. Aaron Weiss, executive director of the Center for Western Priorities, an environmental group, called the idea that Colorado’s regulations explain the sluggish production “nonsense.” He pointed to what oil executives tell investors about keeping spending in check and returning money to shareholders. “At the end of the day, it’s about protecting neighborhoods, protecting families, protecting public health,” Weiss said. “There’s nothing in these regulations that’s actually slowing production. It is entirely a choice that these oil and gas producers are making.”

title: As shop owners face new challenges, they hope Small Business Saturday will boost local support
summary: Colorado small business owners say the annual shopping day, which started in the Great Recession, is as much about building community as it is about supporting local shops.
content: For Morgan Calderini, Small Business Saturday is about sending the message that independent brick-and-mortar shops are no longer just places to buy things. They’re also places where people can gather, learn something new and connect with others. “In this whole sea of buy, buy, buy, support a small business, we just invite people to come down and maybe make something,” Calderini, owner of Ladyfingers Letterpress in Colorado Springs, told CPR News. “Or pick out a card to send to a loved one.” The annual shopping day encourages consumers to support independent businesses. It began more than 15 years ago, when American Express launched the campaign in the wake of the 2008 recession. Ad: “The origin of it is pretty corporate,” Calderini acknowledged. “So, I think it’s an opportunity to think about how we support and where we support.” “For us, Small Business Saturday is really a chance to extend our gratitude to our customers,” she said. Ladyfingers Letterpress is leaning into that idea this year with two drop-in workshops focused on candle-making and journal-making. Courtesy: Morgan Calderini Morgan Calderini holds a coupon from her store, Ladyfingers Letterpress, in Colorado Springs. They will be handed out on Small Business Saturday. At Tangled Ball Yarn in Edgewater, owner Marsha Corn hopes to see a steady stream of customers come through the door Saturday, but she also hopes to give them a place to gather and make their own gifts. “We’ll probably have people hanging out in the store, because people are always hanging out at my tables to knit or crochet, socialize,” she said. “That’s what my store is about.” McKenzie Lange/CPR News Marsha Corn, owner of The Tangled Ball in Edgewater Public Market, shows a knitting kit they will sell during Small Business Saturday. Nov. 25, 2026. Corn has prepared displays of gift ideas to encourage customers to explore the possibilities of crafting, whether they’re making something for themselves or creating a gift for someone else. “It’s good for our souls to craft and make things, to get out of our mind and concentrate on the task at hand instead of everything else going on,” she said. Calderini says the day is also about local businesses supporting each other. McKenzie Lange/CPR News Yarn on sale at The Tangled Ball, which will participate in Small Business Saturday, in Edgewater Public Market. Nov. 25, 2026. Ladyfingers is partnering with other local businesses through a holiday coupon book, which features specials from participating businesses, like a free card with purchases over $6 or a free lavender lemonade at a local restaurant with the purchase of six cards. Meanwhile, Little Blue Pigeon Books in Denver is partnering with four other downtown bookstores on a literary passport program encouraging shoppers to visit each location. “I think small businesses, and especially mine, survive because we support our community, and our community does that for us too,” Paige Dungan, who recently opened the book shop, said. “I truly believe that (we) — especially independent bookstores — offer a space for everyone to feel seen, wanted, and connected either with a story or a person.” McKenzie Lange/CPR News A passerby walks past Little Blue Pigeon Books in Larimer Square. Nov. 25, 2026. Dungan hopes the program will help people explore and introduce them to the independent businesses that make their towns unique. Still, in an era of new economic challenges, the financial upside of the shopping holiday continues to hold value to store owners. Corn said Small Business Saturday accounted for a significant share of Tangled Ball Yarn’s holiday shopping weekend revenue. McKenzie Lange/CPR News A map of bookstores inside Little Blue Pigeon Books in Larimer Square shows a map of stores participating in a literary passport book for Small Business Saturday. Nov. 25, 2026. “Most of my business will be on Small Business Saturday in the next three days,” she said. “So last year we did, probably 25% to 30% more on Small Business Saturday than we did on Black Friday.” For Megan Alfaro on the Western Slope, Small Business Saturday is the biggest sales day of the year at her store, Colorado Baby. “It’s a really fun day,” she said. “I love Small Business Saturday because you don’t have to entice people to come in.” Stina Sieg/CPR News Megan Alfaro, owner of Colorado Baby, stands for a portrait inside the store in downtown Grand Junction. Alfaro says Small Business Saturday is her busiest day of the year. One of the things she appreciates most is customers coming in because they want to support independent businesses, rather than looking for a discount. Even with the financial reality, Dungan said she doesn’t set sales goals for the day because money isn’t her sole mission. “What I like to say is Small Business Saturday is about humans really getting to know one another and connecting by heart first and product second,” she said. “Hopefully it’s a reminder that small business is out here, that not everything needs to be bought online or by a big box store,” Corn said. “We’re doing fine financially. We’re okay. So what it is, for me, is the continuation of building a community, supporting a community, creating friendships. That’s what the day is about.” McKenzie Lange/CPR News People shop at Edgewater Public Market ahead of Small Business Saturday. Nov. 25, 2026.
